Hello everyone, today we will discuss common voltage-related issues in North American low-voltage power grids. First, we’ll introduce the definition of low voltage and its application guidelines. Next, we’ll explore the difference between rated voltage and equipment nameplate voltage. Finally, we’ll explain precautions for using imported equipment.

Next, we will explore the definition of North American low-voltage power grids and their application guidelines.

According to the Canadian Electrical Code and the National Electrical Code (US), voltages below 750 volts are defined as low voltage. Meanwhile, the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) considers voltages of 600 volts and below as low voltage.

In addition to the definition of low voltage, there are several common voltage-related definitions: nominal voltage, system voltage. Both system voltage and nominal voltage generally refer to the voltage in a power supply system, with identical meanings. There is also working voltage, which is the actual measured voltage at the load end of the system, and nameplate voltage.

The relationships between these voltage definitions are as follows: Nominal voltage and working voltage must comply with the voltage drop requirements specified in regulations, meaning the working voltage should not fall below 95% of the nominal voltage. The Canadian Electrical Code (CEC) and the National Electrical Code (NEC) share consistent requirements on this matter.

Another important relationship to note is the matching between working voltage and nameplate voltage. This requires special attention during equipment operation and is typically determined by the equipment’s performance specifications. The voltage difference between working voltage and nameplate voltage should generally not exceed 5%, with a maximum allowable deviation of 10%.

Excessively high or low working voltages are detrimental to equipment. For example, in motor-driven equipment, excessively low voltage can prevent startup and cause winding overheating, while excessively high voltage can compromise insulation. However, cases where working voltage exceeds nominal voltage are relatively rare due to inherent system voltage drops.

Next, we will introduce the low-voltage rating levels and equipment nameplate voltage levels in North America.

Next, we will introduce the low-voltage rating levels and equipment nameplate voltage levels in North America.

Regarding system rated voltages, three-phase systems primarily include voltage levels such as 120V, 208V, 277/480V, and 347/600V. Among these, 120/208V is used in both the United States and Canada. The 277/480V level is more common in the U.S., while in Canada, it is mainly employed in industrial sectors like oil fields and semiconductor manufacturing. The 347/600V level is uncommon in the U.S., where 277/480V is predominantly used. Additionally, the Split Phase voltage level of 120/240V is primarily utilized in residential projects, and in rare cases, it may also be applied in three-phase Delta-connected systems.

Equipment nameplate voltages typically differ from the rated voltages of the power supply system. For example, single-phase 115V, three-phase 208V, three-phase 460V, three-phase 575V, and split phase voltages ranging from 220V to 230V. This is because the nameplate voltage of electrical equipment is usually about 5% lower than the corresponding rated voltage in the power supply system, which aligns with the NEC or CEC requirement that voltage drop should not exceed 5%.

The Split Phase system is closely related to most people’s daily lives. Residential buildings commonly use Split Phase power supply systems, while some household appliances operate on two-phase power. Two-phase power is divided into two scenarios: 240V two-phase and 208V two-phase. For instance, single-family homes use 240V two-phase, whereas large apartment complexes employ 208V two-phase due to their three-phase incoming voltage. When purchasing household appliances (such as stoves, water heaters, heat pumps, etc.), the nameplate voltage is typically labeled around 220V or 230V. In reality, such equipment can operate on both 208V two-phase and 240V two-phase systems. Since residential appliances are more affordable than commercial equipment, they are more favored by consumers.

The bottom left corner shows a Split Phase system, while the bottom right displays a three-phase 240V system using Delta connection. Finally, we will discuss voltage compatibility considerations when importing equipment from countries like China for use in Canada.

First, it must be clarified that imported equipment must obtain CSA certification. The specific process for CSA certification has been detailed in other lectures and will not be reiterated here.

Additionally, the equipment must be compatible with a 60Hz power supply system, as China uses 50Hz while North America operates at 60Hz. Equipment imported from China is typically designed for 220/380V voltage systems, which are not standard in North American power grids. Therefore, a transformer must be installed to convert the North American voltage system to 220/380V for direct use with Chinese imported equipment.
